conceptTag: Raise prices at a hair salon
readerTitle: Your salon is fully booked. Is it time to charge more?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (미용실, 골판지 상자 제조사) + 실제 연구 (Kahneman·Knetsch·Thaler 1986 공정성 조사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가격 인상은 '얼마를 올릴까'와 '어떻게 알릴까' 두 질문으로 나눠 판단한다. 첫째는 손님을 몇 명까지 잃어도 되는지 계산하는 문제이고, 둘째는 공정하게 느껴지게 만드는 문제다.
misconception: 단골이 한 명이라도 떠나면 가격 인상은 손해다. 이유를 굳이 설명하지 않고 조용히 올리는 편이 낫다.

sources.text: Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., & Thaler, R. (1986). Fairness as a Constraint on Profit Seeking: Entitlements in the Market. American Economic Review, 76(4), 728–741.
미용실·상자 제조사 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 미용실 계산: 커트 $60, 커트당 변동비 $15(재료·카드 수수료 등) → 남는 돈 $45. 10% 인상 후 $66 − $15 = $51. 이익 손익분기: 100건 × $45 = $4,500, $4,500 ÷ $51 = 88.2건 → 약 11.8%(약 12%, 대략 8명 중 1명)까지 잃어도 같은 돈. 매출 기준 손익분기: $6,000 ÷ $66 = 90.9건 → 약 9.1%(11명 중 1명). 선택지 B·C 수치와 일치하는지 다시 확인.
Kahneman·Knetsch·Thaler(1986) 눈삽 사례: 눈보라 뒤 눈삽 가격 인상을 응답자 대부분(원문 82%)이 불공정하다고 답함. 비용 상승을 가격에 반영하는 것은 대체로 수용 가능하다고 판단. 카드에는 '대부분'으로만 적었음. 원문으로 재확인.
소프트웨어 노트의 '사전 공지·기존 고객 유예 기간' 관행은 일반적 설명이며 특정 기업 사례를 들지 않았음.

cards.title: Your salon is fully booked. Is it time to charge more?
body: Every chair is booked three weeks out. Your prices haven't moved in three years. Rent is up and hair color costs more than it did.
Still, adding $6 to a $60 haircut feels risky. What if your regulars walk?

image.label: A salon appointment book with every slot filled
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 동네 미용실 카운터 위에 펼쳐진 예약 장부, 3주치 칸이 모두 손글씨로 꽉 차 있음. 옆에 "$60" 가격표와 가위. 실제 브랜드 로고나 제품 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How many clients could you lose?
body: Each haircut costs you about $15 in supplies, card fees and products used. You plan to raise the price 10%, from $60 to $66.
How many clients could leave before you earn *less* than today?

options.text: Almost none. Every lost client hurts
options.feedback: This fear keeps prices frozen for years. A raise adds to every remaining cut, so you can lose some clients and still come out ahead.
That's where your *sales* stay the same. But a client who leaves also takes away the $15 you spend on them, so your margin for error is wider.
Right. This is the core of **Raising prices**: what you keep per cut rises from $45 to $51, so you can lose almost 12% of cuts and still earn the same.

cards.title: Follow 100 haircuts.
body: The $6 raise goes straight to what you keep, so that number grows 13%, not 10%. And with a three-week wait, clients who leave free up chairs for people already waiting.

cards.title: A full book is a price signal.
body: When demand is higher than the hours you can sell, your price is probably below what many clients would pay. A long waitlist is the clearest sign.

That's the lesson from **Raising prices** applied here: the question isn't whether anyone will leave. It's whether the people who stay make up for those who go. With a full book, lost clients may cost you almost nothing.
Smaller, regular raises also beat one big jump after years of waiting.

cards.title: How do you tell your regulars?
body: You've decided on $66. Now you need to announce it.

options.text: Put up a new price sign on the day it changes
options.feedback: It's quick, but a surprise at the register feels like being caught out. Even a fair price can feel unfair when nobody warned you.

options.text: Tell each regular a month ahead: costs are up, and prices haven't changed in three years
options.feedback: This is **Perceived fairness** at work. Notice gives people time, and a cost reason feels like sharing a burden, not taking advantage.

options.text: Post honestly: "We're in high demand, so prices are going up"
options.feedback: It's true and it's the real reason. But a rise tied to demand tends to feel like profiting from loyalty, while a rise tied to costs feels earned.

cards.title: People judge the reason, not just the price.
body: In a 1986 survey, Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler asked people about a store that raised the price of snow shovels after a snowstorm. Most called it unfair. Yet passing on higher costs was widely seen as acceptable.
Your clients use the same test. Same $6, different story, different reaction.

image.label: Two price tags: one tied to costs, one tied to demand
image.brief: 두 개의 가격표를 나란히. 왼쪽 "+$6 · Our costs went up" 옆에 끄덕이는 손님, 오른쪽 "+$6 · You can't get in anyway" 옆에 팔짱 낀 손님. 따뜻한 파스텔 톤, 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: Software companies face the same test. Advance notice, a clear reason, and sometimes a period at the old price for existing users make a raise feel earned rather than taken.

cards.title: The 12% cushion has conditions.
body: It assumes clients leave one by one. If a stylist quits and takes her regulars, or a cheaper salon opens nearby with open chairs, losses can pass 12% fast.
Your stylists also deliver the news face to face. Give them the reason in one sentence so they don't apologize or improvise.
And a cost reason sets an expectation. If costs fall later, clients will remember why you said prices rose.

cards.title: Now you make cardboard boxes.
body: Your small factory supplies shipping boxes to local shops. Paper prices have risen and you haven't changed prices in two years. One customer buys 30% of your output.

options.text: Quietly switch to thinner board at the same price
options.feedback: It avoids a hard conversation now. But buyers notice weaker boxes, and a hidden change feels far less fair than an open one.

options.text: Raise 8% for everyone, with 60 days' notice and the paper costs shown
options.feedback: Check the math from **Raising prices**, then pass the **Perceived fairness** test: notice plus a visible cost reason. Business buyers expect cost-based increases.

options.text: Raise prices for small customers only and spare the big one
options.feedback: It protects your largest relationship. But small shops end up carrying the cost, and if they find out, the unequal treatment feels unfair.

cards.title: Do the math, then tell the story.
body: Two ideas did the work. **Raising prices:** figure out how many customers you can lose before a raise costs you. **Perceived fairness:** give notice and a cost reason so the raise feels earned.
**Try it today:** take your main product. Work out what you keep per sale now and after a 10% raise, then divide one by the other. That's how much volume you can lose.
